Crypto trading activity is declining:

Daily trading volume across the 44 spot crypto exchanges tracked by Kaiko fell to ~$15 billion last week, the lowest level of the year.

This marks a -70% decline from January peak levels.

By comparison, in February, there were 2 trading days when volume exceeded $100 billion.

As a result, the average daily volume trend has fallen -50% since December 2025, to $20 billion, the lowest this year.

Meanwhile, trading volume remains heavily concentrated, with the 6 largest exchanges accounting for more than 60% of total activity.

Crypto market liquidity is drying up.

Semiconductor stocks are facing one of their most volatile periods in history:

The semiconductor index, $SOX, saw intraday swings of at least 2% in all 22 trading days in July, matching the reading last seen in 2020.

Before that, such a period last occurred during the 2008 Financial Crisis.

This comes as $SOX fell -21% in July, its worst monthly performance since October 2008, erasing $2.2 trillion from the index's market cap.

As a result, 60-day realized volatility on the index surged to ~66%, the highest since the 2020 pandemic, when it peaked at ~85%.

By comparison, volatility reached ~75% during the 2008 Financial Crisis.

Semiconductor stocks are seeing crisis-level volatility.

Leveraged ETFs in chip stocks are seeing historic capital flows.

Global leveraged and inverse ETFs tracking SK Hynix now hold ~$5.5 billion in assets, the most of any single stock worldwide.

This is followed by Micron, $MU, and Nvidia, $NVDA, which account for ~$5.1 billion and ~$4.8 billion in leveraged and inverse ETF assets, respectively.

By comparison, Tesla, $TSLA, is the largest non-chip name on the list, with ~$3.7 billion tied to the stock.

In total, semiconductor-related names account for ~$21.0 billion in leveraged and inverse ETF assets.

Meanwhile, the 3x leveraged US semiconductor ETF, $SOXL, attracted +$6.9 billion in inflows in July, the largest monthly intake in the fund’s history.

Chip stocks have become the center of leveraged ETF exposure.

Hedge funds are rushing back into tech stocks:

In the week ending Thursday, hedge funds recorded their largest purchase of US technology stocks since December 2022.

This also marked the 3rd-largest weekly purchase in at least 5 years.

The move was primarily driven by long additions, followed by short covering.

Software, semiconductor, and semiconductor equipment stocks saw the strongest demand, followed by tech hardware names.

Furthermore, hedge funds purchased Magnificent 7 stocks for 4 consecutive days ending Thursday.

Hedge funds are piling back into tech.

AI benchmarking is becoming a multi-billion dollar industry.

As the number of AI models multiplies, benchmarking is becoming its own market.

This market now stands at ~$1.2 billion and is expected to grow to $9.6 billion by 2035.

This also implies over ~8x growth over then next ten years.

Instead of judging a model on a fixed benchmark score, companies now want proof that it performs well against real people in real conditions.

In the next phase of AI, it will not be enough to simply build the best models.

The companies that can accurately measure and compare them may become just as critical to the ecosystem.

US business investment in software remains robust.

In Q1 2026, US businesses invested an annualized $797.6 billion in software. 

That is nearly 2x the pace seen a decade ago and one of the highest levels on record.

As AI adoption accelerates, software is increasingly becoming core infrastructure rather than a discretionary expense.

In our view, this reflects the next phase of the AI boom.

It will no longer be about simply building new AI models.

Rather, it will be about companies investing trillions of dollars to deploy these models across various industries.
